passage: By her third week at the restaurant in Manchester, nobody had said Fatima's name. Head Chef's rule: apprentices are 'Commis', they eat standing after everyone else, and they don't use the staff room. Ada, the sous chef, enforced it with a tired shrug. "Commis, bins. Commis, move." When Fatima sat down once on an upturned crate, Ada said, "Up. Not my rule. I'd get it in the neck." At home Fatima caught herself thinking of her hands as equipment, like the mop. She wrote her own name on a sticky note just to see it. On Friday she rang her college tutor, Mr Hughes, and told him everything. He listened, said, "That's not training, that's being treated like a thing," and emailed the restaurant's owner before she had even hung up.

qa.q: What were apprentices called in the kitchen?
qa.a: Apprentices are 'Commis', so nobody said Fatima's name.

qa.q: What does writing her own name on a sticky note suggest Fatima was feeling?
qa.a: Fatima felt invisible and reduced to equipment, like the mop, and needed to remind herself she was a person.

qa.q: What choice made a difference for Fatima, and how did the tutor respond?
qa.a: Fatima rang Mr Hughes and told him everything; he listened, called it being treated like a thing, and emailed the owner straight away.

qa.q: How does Ada seem to see the rule?
qa.a: Ada treats it as Head Chef's rule, not a personal choice, and fears getting in trouble, even while enforcing it with a tired shrug.

grounding: Shows a junior worker stripped of her name under a head chef's rule enforced by staff who insist it isn't theirs.

passage: Room numbers, not names: that was the 'intro week' rule at the girls' hostel, handed down by Neelam, the senior-most resident. For five nights Gargi was '212'. At dinner seniors called out, "212, stand." "212, sing." "212, explain why you're slow." When Gargi asked one of them, a gentle-looking third-year, why, the girl wouldn't meet her eyes. "Neelam di's orders. If we don't, we get it next." By Friday Gargi had stopped looking up from her plate. She felt like a number on a door, something to be moved about. That night she walked to the warden's office in her slippers and said, "I need to report something." The warden closed the door, listened to all of it, said, "This is ragging, and none of it is on you," and phoned the anti-ragging committee head from the desk while Gargi sat there.

qa.q: What number was Gargi called for five nights?
qa.a: For five nights Gargi was '212'.

qa.q: How was Gargi feeling by Friday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Gargi felt like a number on a door, something to be moved about; she had stopped looking up from her plate.

qa.q: Which step turned things around, and what did the warden do?
qa.a: Gargi went to the warden's office to report it; the warden listened, called it ragging, said none of it was on Gargi, and phoned the anti-ragging committee head right then.

qa.q: How does the third-year seem to see her own part in it?
qa.a: She seems uncomfortable, not meeting Gargi's eyes, and insists she has no choice because refusing would make her the next target.

grounding: Illustrates a fresher reduced to a room number by seniors following the senior-most resident's orders, and an adult acting the same night.

passage:
Farida,
I need to tell someone who isn't at the call centre. Our team lead has a new 'accountability' policy: whoever has the lowest call score each day gets their name on the red board, and the rest of the team has to read out their mistakes at the evening huddle. This week it's been me three times. Yesterday people I eat lunch with read out my 'errors' like a list of charges. Afterwards Rukhsar whispered, 'Sorry yaar, TL's policy, we have no choice.' Everyone says that. Nobody looks at me, only at the board. I've started to feel like a score, not a person.
I'm going to HR tomorrow at nine, and I'm printing the huddle messages tonight. Will you call me after? Just to hear a voice that uses my name.
Deepika

qa.q: What happens to the person with the lowest call score each day?
qa.a: Their name goes on the red board, and the rest of the team has to read out their mistakes at the evening huddle.

qa.q: What does 'Just to hear a voice that uses my name' reveal about Deepika?
qa.a: Deepika feels lonely and reduced to a score, and longs to be treated as a person again by someone who cares.

qa.q: What choice has Deepika made, and why is it a strong one?
qa.a: Deepika is going to HR tomorrow at nine with printed huddle messages, taking the problem to people with power over the policy instead of enduring it.

qa.q: How does Rukhsar seem to feel about reading out Deepika's errors?
qa.a: Rukhsar whispers sorry and blames the TL's policy, suggesting guilt mixed with a belief that there is no choice.

grounding: A junior's letter describes being publicly shamed by colleagues carrying out a team lead's policy and feeling like a score, not a person.

passage: "You asked why I nearly quit the football academy, Rashmi. Here's the real reason. First month, the captain made a rule: we junior boys carry every senior's kit bag and are called 'Boot Boy' instead of our names. The seniors did it to us every evening, laughing. When I asked one of them, Ravi, why, he said, 'Captain's orders, Jeevan. If I don't, I'm on bags too.' That was the line from everyone: no choice. After three weeks I felt like a peg to hang bags on. I stopped using my own name in my head. Then one night I phoned my coach at home and told him everything. He came to the hostel that same night, said none of it was my fault, stopped the rule on the spot, and reported it to the academy director before morning."

qa.q: What were juniors called instead of their names?
qa.a: They were called 'Boot Boy' instead of their names.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel after three weeks of carrying the seniors' bags?
qa.a: He felt worthless and invisible, like a peg to hang bags on, so much that he stopped using his own name in his head.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Phoning his coach and telling everything brought an adult who came that night, said it was not his fault, stopped the rule and reported it, so the harm ended.

qa.q: How did Ravi see his part in the rule?
qa.a: Ravi saw himself as having no choice, following the captain's orders so he would not end up carrying bags himself.

grounding: A junior footballer targeted by seniors on the captain's orders feels treated as a thing, while those doing it insist they have no choice.

passage: I'm Kavitha, and I shared a room with Shalini in our nursing hostel, so I saw this from close up. Our ward in-charge started a new policy: any trainee who made an error had her name read out at handover and was put on nights for a week. The staff nurses carried it out; they'd say, "Sorry, Shalini, orders," and then read her name like a charge sheet. Shalini, twenty-two, was on nights for three weeks straight. She stopped eating breakfast with us. Once I heard her say, "I'm just the mistake trainee," in a flat voice. I don't know everything she felt, but she looked at people as if she were furniture being moved. One evening I walked her to the principal's office. The principal listened to her for an hour, said the policy was not how anyone should be treated, and called the ward in-charge in that same evening.

qa.q: What happened to a trainee who made an error under the new policy?
qa.a: Her name was read out at handover and she was put on nights for a week.

qa.q: What does Shalini's flat 'I'm just the mistake trainee' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels worthless and defeated, having started to see herself the way the policy treats her, as a label rather than a person.

qa.q: Which choice by Kavitha made a difference, and why?
qa.a: Walking Shalini to the principal's office brought the problem to someone with power, who listened, rejected the policy and called in the ward in-charge that evening.

qa.q: How did the staff nurses see their own part in the policy?
qa.a: They acted as if they had no choice, saying 'Sorry, Shalini, orders' before reading out her name.

grounding: A trainee targeted by a punitive policy carried out on a superior's orders feels treated as a thing, while those enforcing it insist they are only following orders.
